lesson.title: By Any Means Necessary: The Journeys of Malcolm X
lesson.summary: From a childhood marked by racial violence to his rise as a fiery minister of the Nation of Islam and his final years advocating a broader vision of human rights, Malcolm X offered a sharp and evolving counterpoint to the mainstream civil rights movement's philosophy of nonviolent integration.
lesson.body:
Malcolm Little was born on May 19, 1925, in Omaha, Nebraska. His father, Earl Little, was a Baptist preacher and an organizer for Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association, a Black nationalist movement that had flourished in part out of the cultural pride and confidence associated with the Harlem Renaissance. The family was harassed by white supremacist groups, and Earl Little died in an incident officially ruled an accident when Malcolm was six years old, though the family believed he had been murdered. His mother was later institutionalized, and Malcolm spent part of his childhood in foster care.

As a young man he moved through Boston and then Harlem, drifting into criminal activity that led to his imprisonment in the mid-1940s on burglary charges. In prison he converted to the Nation of Islam, a Black separatist religious movement led by Elijah Muhammad that preached Black self-reliance and discipline and practiced a version of Islam distinct from mainstream Sunni tradition. Upon his release he adopted the name Malcolm X, the X standing for the African family name lost to slavery.

He rose to become the Nation of Islam's most prominent minister, based largely out of its Harlem temple, drawing large crowds with speeches that condemned white supremacy and, notably, questioned the nonviolent, integrationist strategy associated with leaders like Martin Luther King Jr., a strategy that had also drawn hope from the promise of Brown v. Board of Education a decade earlier. Malcolm argued that integration into a still-racist society was not the answer. He called instead for Black economic self-sufficiency, cultural pride, separation from white society, and the right to self-defense, famously insisting on freedom "by any means necessary" rather than a strict commitment to nonviolence.

In 1964 he broke publicly with Elijah Muhammad and the Nation of Islam, amid both personal and doctrinal disputes. That year he completed the Hajj, the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca, and adopted the name el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz. Praying alongside Muslims of many races during the pilgrimage reportedly softened some of his views on the possibility of interracial cooperation, even as he continued to emphasize Black self-determination and framed the struggle increasingly as a matter of human rights, one he hoped to bring before the United Nations. He founded Muslim Mosque, Inc. and the Organization of Afro-American Unity to pursue this broader vision.

On February 21, 1965, Malcolm X was assassinated while speaking at the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem, killed by gunmen connected to the bitter split with the Nation of Islam. Three men were convicted in 1966. In 2021, after a lengthy reinvestigation, two of them, Muhammad A. Aziz and the late Khalil Islam, were formally exonerated when new evidence showed neither had been present at the shooting. Malcolm X's emphasis on Black pride, self-defense, and self-determination would soon find powerful expression in the Black Power movement that emerged in the years after his death.
